values.value: • Recap the requirement, success outcome, timeline, and users back to the buyer in one mail. • Get written confirmation on scope, deliverables, commercials assumptions, and decision path. • Turn the requirement into a solution note tailored to the client's L&D or academic context. • Identify one proof point or case study that mirrors this requirement closely. • Use the clarity you have to move the deal to buyer alignment, not just vendor response.
1|Fully Clear
Buyer may say, 'Just send the proposal.' Response: 'Happy to. I will tailor it around the exact scope and success outcome we aligned on so it moves faster internally.'
You have the brief. Lock the use case, success measure, and buyer pain in writing before the next step.
Low risk. Keep control and avoid scope drift.
Say: 'Let me recap the problem, scope, and success outcome so we stay aligned.'
Fully Clear

• Book a short discovery call only to close the missing requirement gaps. • Ask for current process, learner/user group, scale, success metric, and rollout expectation. • Convert vague asks into measurable outcomes such as adoption, completion, score lift, or turnaround time. • Send a simple checklist after the call and get buyer confirmation in writing. • Hold demo or proposal until the unknowns are closed.
1|Partially clear
Buyer may say, 'You already know enough.' Response: 'I know the broad need. I just want to close the few open points so I do not send you something that misses the mark.'
Run a short discovery call and close every gap before demo or proposal. Do not fill blanks with assumptions.
Risk: Partial clarity leads to weak demos and rework.
Ask: 'What are the must-have outcomes, timeline, users, and non-negotiables here?'
Partially clear

• Stop building solution detail until the missing requirement inputs are received. • Send a tight question list instead of a long note so the buyer can respond quickly. • Prioritise must-knows first: scope, timeline, stakeholders, expected outcome, and buying criteria. • Offer a 15-minute working session to fill the gaps together. • Once the gaps are closed, re-position your solution around their stated needs.
1|Yet to get some from the customer
Buyer may say, 'Please share something first.' Response: 'I can, but even a quick 10-minute clarification now will save both of us a lot of rework later.'
Pause the pitch and get the missing requirement details first. A fast checklist works better than another long deck.
Risk: You are selling with missing facts.
Ask: 'Before I propose anything, can we spend 15 minutes to complete the missing requirement points?'
Yet to get some from the customer

• Do not progress the deal as a solution discussion yet. • Re-open the conversation around the business problem, learner pain, operational challenge, or assessment gap. • Find the owner of the requirement and ask how this need surfaced. • Understand who is affected, what is broken today, and what success must look like. • Only after this, move back into fit, demo, or proposal.
1|Don't know
Buyer may say, 'Send a standard deck for now.' Response: 'I can share context material, but before I suggest a solution I need to understand the actual problem so I do not waste your time.'
Do not progress this deal yet. First understand the requirement, owner, and expected outcome from the buyer side.
High risk: No requirement clarity means a blind deal.
Ask: 'Can you walk me through the problem, who it affects, and what success should look like?'
Don't know
Have you received/understood the Requirements / RFQ from the customer ?
